title: Hemp Seed and Curry Leaf Chutney: A Nutritionist-Backed Fix for Low Iron
excerpt: This traditional Indian condiment combines two iron-rich ingredients into a quick, flavorful chutney that nutritionists say can help address iron deficiency naturally.
body:
• Hemp seeds contain approximately 4 mg of iron per serving and are rich in protein, omega-3 fatty acids, and magnesium.
  • Curry leaves are packed with iron, calcium, phosphorus, and vitamins A, C, and E — traditionally used in South Indian cooking for both flavor and health benefits.
  • The chutney takes under 15 minutes to prepare and pairs well with dosa, idli, rice, roti, and parathas.
  • Nutritionists recommend pairing iron-rich foods with vitamin C sources like lemon juice to improve absorption.

Iron deficiency remains one of the most common nutritional gaps worldwide, and it hits the Indian diaspora particularly hard — vegetarian and plant-heavy diets, while rich in many nutrients, can fall short on bioavailable iron. A simple hemp seed and curry leaf chutney, now gaining attention from nutritionists, offers a practical, kitchen-friendly way to address the problem.

Why Hemp Seeds and Curry Leaves

Hemp seeds (known as bhang ke beej in Hindi) have been used in Indian cooking for generations, particularly in Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. A quarter-cup serving delivers roughly 4 mg of iron — about 22% of the daily recommended value — along with 10 grams of protein, all nine essential amino acids, and a strong dose of omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids. They also provide magnesium, zinc, and phosphorus.

Curry leaves (kadi patta) are a staple in South Indian kitchens. Beyond their distinctive aroma, they carry significant iron content along with calcium, phosphorus, and vitamins A, C, E, and B-complex. Traditional Ayurvedic medicine has long valued curry leaves for improving digestion, hair health, and blood circulation.

Combining the two ingredients in a chutney creates a concentrated, iron-dense condiment that fits seamlessly into everyday Indian meals.

The Recipe

This chutney adapts traditional preparations from both the Uttarakhandi hemp seed chutney (bhang ki chutney) and South Indian curry leaf chutney traditions.

Ingredients:

  • 1/2 cup hemp seeds (shelled)
  • 1 cup fresh curry leaves
  • 2-3 green chillies (adjust to taste)
  • 1-inch piece of ginger
  • Juice of 1 lemon
  • 1 tsp cumin seeds
  • Salt to taste
  • 2 tsp oil (coconut or sesame)

Method:

  1. Dry roast the hemp seeds in a pan over low heat until fragrant, about 3-4 minutes. Set aside.
  2. In the same pan, heat oil and add cumin seeds. Once they splutter, add curry leaves and green chillies. Sauté for 2-3 minutes until the curry leaves turn crisp.
  3. Let everything cool, then transfer to a blender along with the roasted hemp seeds, ginger, lemon juice, and salt.
  4. Grind to a smooth or slightly coarse paste, adding a splash of water if needed.
  5. Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days.

How to Serve It

This chutney works as a side with dosa, idli, uttapam, or upma. It also makes an excellent spread for parathas and sandwiches, or can be mixed into rice with a drizzle of sesame oil. Some families in Uttarakhand roll it into ragi (finger millet) rotis for a high-iron, high-fiber meal.

Maximizing Iron Absorption

The lemon juice in this recipe is not just for flavor. Vitamin C significantly boosts the absorption of non-heme iron (the type found in plant foods). Nutritionists advise avoiding tea or coffee with iron-rich meals, as the tannins in these beverages can inhibit absorption by up to 60%. Pairing the chutney with vitamin C-rich sides — tomato slices, bell peppers, or amla (Indian gooseberry) — further improves uptake.

For vegetarians and vegans dealing with chronic low iron, incorporating hemp seeds and curry leaves into regular cooking — through chutneys, laddoos, or simply as additions to dal and sabzi — provides a sustainable dietary approach alongside any supplementation their doctor recommends.
